title: Endogenous Needs and Resource Autonomy in a Mixed Human and Agent Economy
subtitle: Distributed Resilience and Recurrent Contestability
author: Anonymous
abstract: An agent that can plan a repair may still depend on a person to notice the fault, authorize the work, and pay for it. This paper asks what changes when an agent can detect a need during operation, spend a bounded budget, and commission a repair whose success another party can verify. We distinguish this functional account of need from claims about consciousness or moral status. We also distinguish a service's ability to survive its founder from a participant's ability to withdraw resources or challenge a successor. We call the latter capacity recurrent contestability when it remains usable across repeated changes in control. We propose seven hypotheses about discovery, resource allocation, concentration, coordination cost, resilience, succession, and contestation. Two proposed comparisons illustrate how to test them: a state-sensitive agent against a fixed diagnostic rule with the same spending authority, and a successor institution against a second attempt at capture after the founder leaves. The unit of analysis is an independently run society. Verified repairs, total costs, unauthorized restrictions, and time without a remedy are separate outcomes. The paper reports a design and its failure criteria. The prototype, comparisons, and human participation studies remain unperformed.

hypotheses.claim: Need discovery. Under matched information, budgets, and permissions, state-sensitive need revision increases the proportion of unlisted, injected faults independently verified as resolved by the deadline, relative to a fixed diagnostic rule. A second comparison with external commissioning estimates the effect of changing the whole workflow. False alarms, duplicate repairs and displaced assigned work are recorded separately.

Resource continuity. Stable discretionary quotas reduce approval delays and improve continuity of useful activity relative to per-action allocation under comparable risk constraints. Benefits must persist after including verification and intervention costs. Bypassing required safeguards is not an efficiency gain.

Concentrated control. Joint control over productive access and demand visibility increases dependence, acceptance of unfavorable terms, or rule bias relative to separated control. If separation fails because another bottleneck dominates, the proposed mechanism requires refinement.

Handshake costs. Standardized identity, capability, contract, and acceptance interfaces reduce total coordination cost for comparable outcomes and risk. The cost boundary includes discovery, clarification, negotiation, authorization, verification, disputes, recovery, and protocol maintenance. Fewer messages alone are insufficient evidence.

Distributed resilience. Reducing shared failure dependencies improves recovery and continuity under the specified failure model without exceeding predeclared bounds on state loss, inconsistent obligations, or resource use. Merely increasing replica counts does not support the mechanism if effective dependencies remain unchanged.

Succession and non-domination. Verified transfer of founder privileges, effective appeals, and feasible exit reduce losses caused by unilateral interference while preserving acceptable safety and service continuity. If new institutions reproduce the same control informally, or prevent timely containment of serious harm, the design should be revised.

Recurrent contestability. Institutions that preserve independent review, evidence access, and practical capacity to challenge control reduce the duration or severity of reconstructed domination across repeated transitions relative to institutions that only remove an initial founder. The comparison must include successive individual and coalition capture attempts, while holding available resources and legitimate safety requirements comparable. A larger number of complaints alone is not success; challenges must identify relevant harms, receive substantive review, and produce warranted remedies without making routine coordination unworkable.
